subject: Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?

messages.author: 269e905d87d26565
messages.subject: Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?
parts:
Hello,

I have a F1 progeny from two outbred parents (4way cross then) with no missing genotype information and with around 600 markers. R propose 4 methods for interval mapping (em, imp, haley-knott and extended haley-knott)

I wanted to know if I should do the QTL detection with the EM method proposed in R or if another method would fit better than this one for my case. I thought about the multiple imputation method but as I don't have missing genotyping data, I am not sure I need it.
Furthermore, i would like to perform after that a QTL detection with Multiple QTL Mapping and i read that "multiple imputation (imp method) has greatest value for the fit and exploration of MQM models". So I am a little lost in the choice of the method for the first step of my qtl detection.

 Could you give any advice according your experience ? How do/did you do to choose between the method ? 
This would really help me because i would like to understand the way that scientists choose their method so I can make a reasonable and thoughful decision for my analysis.

Thanks

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?
parts:
For a detailed discussion of the relative advantage of the different methods for handling missing data, see chapter 4 of the R/qtl book (https://rqtl.org/book).

In a typical 4-way cross, many markers would be less-than-fully informative. It's hard to know, from the information you've provided, whether 600 markers is a lot or not, and it partly depends on how they are distributed across the genome. Are there any regions with gaps. plotInfo() can be useful for assessing the amount of missing genotype information.

If you're interested in fitting multiple-QTL models, you might start with the multiple imputation approach. With more imputations [n.draws in sim.geno()] everything takes more time and memory but does a better job of dealing with missing genotype information. If you repeat analyses (sim.geno and then scanone) and get rather different results, you likely need to increase n.draws.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?
parts:
> Nevertheless, I run plotInfo() and I got this plot. There is some large regions with no markers (specially in chromosome 2) but the distribution of the markers in the Linkage groups is pretty good to me. What i don't understand (even after reading the guide) is why the misinfo.entropy starts at 0,5 and not 0. Is it because as you said the markers in 4way cross are not fully informative ? I am also working in a female and male map separately, can that be the reason ?

It has something to do with the nature of the markers, but I‘m not entirely sure how. When you say “working in a female and male map separately”, do you mean that you’re working with just the markers segregating in one parent and not the other? That would explain it, as you’d always be missing at least half of the information.

I think it’d be better to integrate the information from all markers. And if you’re going to use markers segregating in just one parent, it’s probably best to treat it as a backcross (“bc”) rather than 4-way cross (“4way”).

karl

You should be able to do QTL analysis considering one set of markers, and treating it as a backcross. But I don't have any experience with this.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?
parts:
stepwiseqtl() is seeking the model that optimizes the penalized LOD score, but its search method won't necessarily that find the globally optimal model. And in this case there's an added source of variability, as you've re-run the imputations from sim.geno, and 200 imputations is not sufficient here.

You're treating the cross as "4way" but with markers segregating on just one side? That's not going to work for this analysis. You're fitting a 3 parameters for each QTL and an additional 9 parameters for each QTL:QTL interaction, but you've got information only about the genotype on one chromosome at each QTL.

Also, others have reported that stepwiseqtl() doesn't work properly for cross type "4way", though to be honest I can't remember the nature of the problem.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Is there a preferred method for fitting a single QTL model ?
parts:
I wouldn't suggest using _only_ the markers that are segregating in both parents. But if you want to do QTL analysis with cross type "4way", you'll need some way to integrate the full set of markers. But unfortunately you'd probably need to do more work to identify and genotype additional markers that allow you to integrate the markers.

It's possible that stepwiseqtl() can work with a 4-way cross, but some users have reported errors and we've not been able to track them down and fix them.

Working with markers segregating in one parent and treating it as a backcross is one way to try to do QTL analysis with your data, but I'm not sure that I would recommend it. Certainly you'll need to proceed with caution.

karl
